paras: The Booker murders and attempted lynching at Winchester, Tennessee, were the killing of Simon Booker and his wife at their Franklin County cabin on the night of August 4, 1903, and a mob's attempt six days later to lynch the three men charged with it. Sheriff Jim Stewart took the prisoners to Nashville before the mob reached the jail, and all three were later convicted and hanged at Winchester on May 5, 1904. Early dispatches called the killings moonshiners' revenge on informers, and one Alabama paper headlined the accused as "Three Negroes."

The aged couple lived in a small cabin on the mountain near "Thunderstruck Hollow," in the sixteenth district of Franklin County. According to the first Chattanooga dispatch, a wildcat distillery near their place had been raided in June, and the "wild-catters" accused the Bookers of betraying them to revenue officers. No report gives the couple's race.

A Winchester dispatch to the Columbia Herald said John Evans and "Jo Debb" shot Booker, killed his wife and burned the house, consuming her body. That dispatch had Booker crawling from the flames "at the point of death," while the Bourbon News said he was found unconscious and "has since died."

Henry Judge, Joe Delp and John Evans were arrested, the last on Friday, August 7, and "preparations for a lynching began." On the afternoon of August 10 a "well-organized mob" of 400 men came into Winchester and went to the jail. Warned in advance, Sheriff Stewart had already left with his prisoners by a roundabout route to the railway, and they reached the Davidson County jail in Nashville.

In Nashville Delp confessed that Judge had hired him and Evans after "some trouble about a lumber deal" with Booker, and that Evans did the shooting and set the fire. Judge denied any part, and with the excitement "partially subsided" the men were returned to Winchester, where a grand jury indicted them for murder and arson on August 17.

Delp's trial opened on August 31 before a courtroom "packed to suffocation," and the jury found him guilty of first-degree murder the next day. Delp and Evans were sentenced on September 3, and Judge on September 7, to hang on October 9. Sentencing them, Judge McReynolds said Delp and Evans were "convicted out of their own mouths," though Evans declared he was not guilty.

The hanging took place instead on May 5, 1904, and the coverage does not explain the delay. The Indianapolis Journal reported threats to tear down the scaffold fence so the execution would be public, and said the sheriff set an early hour to prevent trouble.

The first report moved as a Chattanooga special on August 5 and ran in the Montgomery Advertiser and the Atlanta Constitution under headlines such as "Man and Wife Murdered." Weekly digests in Washington and Arkansas reduced it to a sentence blaming "wildcatter distillers" or "moonshiners." The Black press carried only this early wire: the Cleveland Gazette ran it as "Moonshiners Got Revenge" and the Baltimore Afro-American gave it one digest line, both dated "Winchester, Ky." and without comment or a race.

The Birmingham Age-Herald headed the Nashville wire on the mob "HAD NO LYNCHING. Three Negroes Have Close Call From Mountaineers," while the Montgomery Advertiser ran the same text as "MOB IS DISAPPOINTED" with no racial label. The Columbia Herald followed the confession and trial closely, and the 1904 hanging was reported as far as Washington state and Indiana, often naming the victim "Bucher." None of the trial or execution reports mentions race.

Besides the question of whether Booker died at once, the motive shifted from moonshiners' revenge in the first dispatches to Judge's quarrel over lumber or land in Delp's confession. The payment was "over $100" in the jail confession but a promise of ten dollars in the trial testimony, and a 1904 dispatch said Judge wanted timber visible from the couple's land.

reader.title: Booker murders and attempted lynching at Winchester, Tennessee
bases: The only collective violence reported is a mob of 400 that went to the Winchester jail to lynch the three men charged with the Booker murders, who had been removed beforehand (A7); the murders themselves were a hired double killing with arson to conceal it (A2, A13), not arson as the primary act.

Independent dispatches agree on the double murder and burning (A1, A2, A3), and the mob threat is reported in the Nashville wire (A7) and confirmed by later Winchester and Nashville reports that the men were moved 'for fear of mob violence' (A12, A13).

framing.detail: First reports ran as brief wire items such as 'Man and Wife Murdered' blaming 'wild-catters'.
The Age-Herald headed the mob story 'HAD NO LYNCHING. Three Negroes Have Close Call From Mountaineers', the only racial label in the coverage; the Montgomery reprint used 'MOB IS DISAPPOINTED'.
The Columbia Herald called the murders a 'horrible and shocking double murder' and headed the confession 'MURDER WILL OUT'.
The Cleveland Gazette ran the early wire as 'Moonshiners Got Revenge' and the Afro-American gave it one digest line, both with a Kentucky dateline and no comment.
